title: Modi Pitches Secure, Open Maritime Order as Sagarmanthan Summit Opens in Delhi
excerpt: The third edition of Sagarmanthan: The Great Oceans Dialogue runs October 7–9 with 1,200 delegates from nearly 75 countries, as India positions itself as a convenor on ocean governance amid mounting pressure on global sea lanes.
body:
• The third edition of Sagarmanthan: The Great Oceans Dialogue opened in New Delhi on October 7, bringing more than 1,200 delegates from nearly 75 countries for three days of talks on trade, technology, sustainability and cooperation at sea.
  • In a message to the summit, Prime Minister Narendra Modi pitched India's vision of a "free, open, and secure maritime network" and said the dialogue strengthens the rules-based world order while enhancing peace, trust and friendship between nations.
  • The 2026 edition, themed "Blue Geographies, New Aspirations: Trade, Technology, and Trust at Sea," unfolds against mounting pressure on global sea lanes — from the Strait of Hormuz to the Malacca Strait — where geopolitical tension, climate stress and technological disruption are hitting trade and energy flows.
  • The dialogue feeds into India's Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047, which places ports, shipping and the blue economy at the centre of the country's long-term growth strategy.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday called for a secure, open maritime order as the third edition of Sagarmanthan: The Great Oceans Dialogue opened in New Delhi, drawing more than 1,200 speakers, delegates and participants from nearly 75 countries to deliberate the future of the global maritime sector.

In a special message to the three-day summit, co-hosted by the Observer Research Foundation and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Modi said India's vision of a free, open and secure maritime network — "be it the Indian Ocean or the Indo-Pacific region" — is finding resonance across the world. The Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative, he said, envisions marine resources as a key pillar of growth, and the dialogue strengthens the rules-based world order while enhancing peace, trust and friendship between nations.

"Our vision for a free, open, and secure maritime network — be it the Indian Ocean or the Indo-Pacific region — is finding resonance across the world."

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

A summit against a volatile backdrop

Launched in New Delhi in 2024 and held in Mumbai in 2025 as part of India Maritime Week, Sagarmanthan has grown into India's flagship annual platform for ocean governance. The 2026 edition runs October 7–9 under the theme "Blue Geographies, New Aspirations: Trade, Technology, and Trust at Sea."

The timing is pointed. The dialogue opens as trade, energy, food and critical minerals move through waters increasingly affected by geopolitical tensions, climate stress and technological disruption. ORF's framing is blunt: "From the Strait of Hormuz to the Malacca Strait... the contest over maritime spaces is intensifying even as dependence on them deepens." With tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz making headlines this week and the Middle East war continuing to snarl energy transit, the question the summit poses — whether the world can secure its oceans before instability defines the global order — is more than rhetorical.

The 2026 edition centres on five thematic pillars: "Steady Straits: Safeguarding Flows in a Fractured World"; "Blue Breakthroughs: Greening Ships and Shipbuilding"; "Complex Seas: Managing Trade, Connectivity, and Turbulence"; "Ocean Societies: Communities, Cultures, and Livelihoods"; and "The Heart of the Deal: Linking Harbour Cities to the Hinterland."

Who is in the room

The guest list reflects the summit's diplomatic ambition. Ministers attending include Belgium's Annick De Ridder, European Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism Apostolos Tzitzikostas, Mauritius's Arvin Boolell, Bhutan's Chandra Bahadur Gurung, Mozambique's João Jorge Matlombe, Lithuania's Juras Taminskas, Greece's Stefanos Gkikas, Myanmar's U Tun Lu and Norway's Astrid Bergmål. Former Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd, former Tunisian Prime Minister Mehdi Jomaa and former Maldives President Mohamed Nasheed are also participating.

The Government of India is represented by Ports, Shipping and Waterways Minister Sarbananda Sonowal, Minister of State Shantanu Thakur and Secretary Vijay Kumar, with Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan also taking part. DP World is the logistics partner, with Konrad Adenauer Stiftung, the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy and Fincantieri on board, and the governments of the Netherlands and Norway partnering through their foreign ministries.

India's maritime pitch

Modi tied the summit to his broader maritime doctrine, invoking India's seafaring heritage — the port cities of Lothal and Dholavira, the fleets of the Chola dynasty, the exploits of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj — and arguing that oceans are "a shared heritage for nations and societies, as well as the lifeline for international trade."

"As we strive to realise the vision of a Viksit Bharat by 2047, dialogues such as Sagarmanthan are invaluable to build consensus, partnerships, and, most importantly, a prosperous future," he said, expressing confidence the discussions would resonate far beyond the conference hall.

The dialogue also aligns with India's Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047, which puts ports, shipping and the blue economy at the heart of the country's long-term growth — a bet that whoever governs the oceans' rules will shape the century's trade.
